chapter: Learning from players; Jonah Jones lessons
title: Dry long so and Ivie Anderson's song
summary: Maxwell recalls a Duke song heard in 1933 and Hinton explains the expression.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Well, you know Duke wrote a tune that I heard in Sacramento in 1933, and I still remember, it's the only time I ever heard it, and the words were, 'I don't finance romancers, I don't romance financiers, I just take things slow and easy, dry long so. So finally I asked Cootie that, five years ago I said, this song -- Ivy Anderson, he got very upset. 'That was my song, I sang it.' I said, well, the night I heard it, she sang it. I said, what the hell does 'dry long so', I don't even know how you spell it, even. He said, well, you know, dry long so, you know -- did you ever hear that expression?
Oh, yes, that's a black expression.
Okay, that's what I thought. I heard --
you know, I remember that from 1933, and I have never heard anybody say it.

It's an old black expression of the '20s, if a guy would say, 'well, how do you do?' 'Dry long so.' He was coming on down the road dry long so. Just taking his time, drinking. I haven't heard it in ages.

Well, you know, because so many black people are uneducated they would have a natural genius for language. They would have been Shakespeare, maybe. So it came out in some of these godawful expressions, the most beautiful expressions you can ever think of. In a way you almost say, I hope they never get educated because --
Some of the creations were so great.
